youtube.title: The Winner Paid the Most and Lost #Shorts
youtube.description:
Ben just won the auction. And he just lost money.

When nobody knows what a prize is really worth, the winning bid tends to come from whoever overestimated it most. That is the winner's curse, named by oil engineers studying offshore lease auctions (Capen, Clapp & Campbell, 1971). In classroom auctions of coin jars worth $8, the average guess was about $5, yet the average winning bid was about $10 (Bazerman & Samuelson, 1983; Thaler, 1988). The fix: bid below your own estimate, and step back further when there are more bidders.

So, would you still raise your paddle?

Sources:
- Thaler (1988), Anomalies: The Winner's Curse, Journal of Economic Perspectives 2(1): https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/jep.2.1.191
- Bazerman & Samuelson (1983), I Won the Auction But Don't Want the Prize, Journal of Conflict Resolution 27(4): https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:sae:jocore:v:27:y:1983:i:4:p:618-634
- Capen, Clapp & Campbell (1971), Competitive Bidding in High-Risk Situations (summary): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winner%27s_curse
- Harvard Program on Negotiation, How to avoid the winner's curse: https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/business-negotiations/how-to-avoid-the-winners-curse

Ben and the school charity auction are fictional.
